title: What is the difference between Comparable.compareTo (natural ordering, defined IN the class) and Comparator.compare (external strategy, defined OUTSIDE), and how does Comparator.naturalOrder() / Comparator.reverseOrder() help?
shortTitle: Comparable.compareTo vs Comparator.compare — natural ordering vs external strategy

s1_definition.profdef: `Comparable<T>` is an interface implemented BY the class itself — it defines the class's NATURAL ordering via `compareTo(T other)`. There is exactly ONE natural ordering per class (e.g., String sorts alphabetically, Integer sorts numerically). `Comparator<T>` is an interface implemented OUTSIDE the class — it defines an EXTERNAL, pluggable sorting strategy via `compare(T a, T b)`. You can have UNLIMITED Comparators for the same class (sort by name, by age, by salary — different strategies). `Comparator.naturalOrder()` returns a Comparator that uses the object's natural ordering (Comparable.compareTo). `Comparator.reverseOrder()` returns the reverse of natural ordering.
s1_definition.analogy: Comparable = the bank's DEFAULT way to sort employees — by employee ID (built INTO the Employee class). There is only ONE default. Comparator = EXTERNAL sorting instructions the manager writes on a piece of paper: "sort by salary descending" or "sort by department then name." The manager can write unlimited different instructions without changing the Employee class. `naturalOrder()` = "sort the default way (by employee ID)." `reverseOrder()` = "sort the default way, but backwards."
s1_definition.oneliner: Comparable = ONE natural order defined IN the class (compareTo). Comparator = MANY external orders defined OUTSIDE (compare). naturalOrder() bridges Comparable to Comparator. reverseOrder() flips natural order.
s1_definition.raw:
**Professional definition:** `Comparable<T>` is an interface implemented BY the class itself — it defines the class's NATURAL ordering via `compareTo(T other)`. There is exactly ONE natural ordering per class (e.g., String sorts alphabetically, Integer sorts numerically). `Comparator<T>` is an interface implemented OUTSIDE the class — it defines an EXTERNAL, pluggable sorting strategy via `compare(T a, T b)`. You can have UNLIMITED Comparators for the same class (sort by name, by age, by salary — different strategies). `Comparator.naturalOrder()` returns a Comparator that uses the object's natural ordering (Comparable.compareTo). `Comparator.reverseOrder()` returns the reverse of natural ordering.

**In simple words (banking analogy):** Comparable = the bank's DEFAULT way to sort employees — by employee ID (built INTO the Employee class). There is only ONE default. Comparator = EXTERNAL sorting instructions the manager writes on a piece of paper: "sort by salary descending" or "sort by department then name." The manager can write unlimited different instructions without changing the Employee class. `naturalOrder()` = "sort the default way (by employee ID)." `reverseOrder()` = "sort the default way, but backwards."

**One line to remember:** Comparable = ONE natural order defined IN the class (compareTo). Comparator = MANY external orders defined OUTSIDE (compare). naturalOrder() bridges Comparable to Comparator. reverseOrder() flips natural order.

sections.s3_banking:
**Problem — The bank's Trade class has a natural ordering by tradeId (chronological).** But different screens need different sorts: the blotter needs sorting by amount descending, the audit trail needs the natural tradeId order, the risk dashboard needs sorting by symbol then amount, and the settlement screen needs sorting by status then date. The team implements Comparable for the natural order (tradeId) and creates four separate Comparator instances for the four screens — without modifying the Trade class for each new sort requirement.

**What the project will show:** Comparable implementation in Trade (compareTo by tradeId), external Comparators (by amount, by symbol+amount, by status), naturalOrder() in nullsLast wrapper, reverseOrder() for descending, and side-by-side demonstration of natural vs external ordering.

sections.s5_journey:
**Step 1 — Natural order.** Trades inserted out of order: TRD-005, TRD-001, TRD-003, TRD-002, TRD-004. `sorted()` uses `Trade.compareTo()` which compares tradeId. Result: TRD-001 through TRD-005 (alphabetical/chronological).

**Step 2 — External order.** Same trades, but `sorted(BY_AMOUNT_DESC)` ignores tradeId. Uses the Comparator that extracts amount and reverses. Result: HDFC(330150), RELIANCE(245050), INFY(222037), TCS(176000), WIPRO(33664).

**Step 3 — naturalOrder() bridge.** `BY_STATUS_THEN_ID` uses `thenComparing(Comparator.naturalOrder())`. After grouping by status, ties within each status group are broken by compareTo (tradeId). naturalOrder() wraps the Trade's compareTo as a Comparator that thenComparing can use.

**Step 4 — TreeSet.** `new TreeSet<>(trades)` automatically uses Trade's natural order (compareTo). Elements stored in tradeId order. `new TreeSet<>(Comparator.comparing(Trade::getAmount))` overrides with external order — stored by amount.

**Step 5 — reverseOrder().** `Comparator.reverseOrder()` returns the reverse of natural ordering. TRD-005 before TRD-001 — opposite of compareTo.
sections.s5b_flow:
```
  ═══ COMPARABLE vs COMPARATOR ═══

  COMPARABLE (natural ordering — IN the class):
    class Trade implements Comparable<Trade> {
        int compareTo(Trade other) { return tradeId.compareTo(other.tradeId); }
    }
    ONE ordering per class. Used by sorted(), TreeSet, Collections.sort().
    Cannot change without modifying the class.

  COMPARATOR (external strategy — OUTSIDE the class):
    Comparator<Trade> byAmount = Comparator.comparing(Trade::getAmount);
    Comparator<Trade> bySymbol = Comparator.comparing(Trade::getSymbol);
    UNLIMITED orderings. No class modification. Passed as parameter.

  ═══ BRIDGING: naturalOrder() + reverseOrder() ═══

  Comparator.naturalOrder()  → wraps compareTo as a Comparator
  Comparator.reverseOrder()  → wraps compareTo reversed

  Used in:
    nullsLast(naturalOrder())           ← nullsLast needs Comparator, not Comparable
    thenComparing(naturalOrder())       ← tiebreak using natural order
    sorted(reverseOrder())              ← reverse natural order

  ═══ WHEN TO USE WHICH ═══

  Comparable: when the class has ONE obvious default order
    String → alphabetical. Integer → numeric. Trade → by tradeId.
    Implement in the class. Used automatically by sorted collections.

  Comparator: when you need MULTIPLE or CUSTOM sort orders
    Sort by amount. Sort by date. Sort by status then amount.
    Defined externally. Passed to sort methods.
```

sections.s6_takeaway:
Comparable defines ONE natural ordering INSIDE the class via `compareTo()`. It is the default for `sorted()`, `TreeSet`, `TreeMap`, and `Collections.sort()`. String's natural order is alphabetical, Integer's is numeric. You implement Comparable when the class has one obvious default sort order. Comparator defines UNLIMITED external ordering strategies OUTSIDE the class via `compare()`. You create Comparators with `Comparator.comparing()`, lambdas, or the fluent chain API. No class modification needed — different screens can use different Comparators for the same data.

In my trade ordering service, Trade implements Comparable with compareTo by tradeId — the natural chronological order. The blotter screen uses `Comparator.comparing(Trade::getAmount).reversed()` for amount descending. The risk dashboard uses `comparing(symbol).thenComparing(amount)`. The settlement screen uses `comparing(status).thenComparing(naturalOrder())` — this last one uses `Comparator.naturalOrder()` to bridge Trade's Comparable.compareTo into the Comparator chain for tiebreaking within each status group.

`Comparator.naturalOrder()` wraps the element's compareTo as a Comparator — essential when APIs need a Comparator but you want natural ordering (e.g., `nullsLast(naturalOrder())`). `Comparator.reverseOrder()` wraps compareTo reversed. In interviews, emphasize: Comparable = one default order, defined once, class must implement. Comparator = many custom orders, defined externally, no class modification. Use Comparable for the primary identity sort, Comparator for everything else.
